quote.text: The hand is the cutting edge of the mind.
quote.author: Jacob Bronowski, The Ascent of Man (1973)

stories.kicker: The Atelier · Eyewear, from the Acetate Up
stories.headline: A Dozen Logos, One Factory Line: Buy the Frame by Its Maker, Not Its Badge
stories.dek: Eyewear is the purest test of this desk's thesis: the material that decides whether a frame lasts costs a rounding error, the hinge that decides its life is invisible on the shelf, and the "designer" name on the temple is usually a licence printed on a mass-produced unit from one of five conglomerates.

stories.kicker: The Good Life · Provenance on the Wrist
stories.headline: A Watch Built on a Fifty-Year-Old Movement, and Signed by the Hand That Saved It
stories.dek: Singer Reimagined's new chronograph does something the spec sheet cannot flatter: it takes a genuine, unused 1970s Valjoux 72 movement, restores and refinishes it to haute-horlogerie standard, and engraves the bridge "Restored by Singer." It is expensive, hand-wound and slow. It is also the weekend's clearest argument for the maker over the number.

stories.headline: The One Flying Machine You Build Yourself, and Fly from Inside
stories.dek: A camera drone flies itself; an FPV quad is flown — no self-levelling, no hover, a live feed piped into goggles so you sit in the cockpit. It is the corner of droning where people still solder their own aircraft, argue about firmware, and crash on purpose to learn. This weekend we go down it: the gear, the money pit, and the hard truth about flying it in Singapore.

stories.kicker: The World · The Strait of Hormuz
stories.headline: Washington Declares an Economic War. Tehran Sends Back a Bill.
stories.dek: Six months into the longest closure of the oil chokepoint on record, Washington has stopped threatening and started naming — a structured sanctions campaign aimed not at Iran alone but at the buyers, banks and shippers that keep it solvent. Iran's reply was not a key to the strait but a bill: compensation, an unfrozen economy, an end to the war.

stories.headline: The Factories Grew Again. The Growth Got Narrower.
stories.dek: July's manufacturing print was another gain — and another quiet warning. The number is carried almost entirely by the AI-chip cycle; strip out electronics and precision engineering and the picture is of clusters going backwards. The relief cheques land next week against an economy leaning hard on a single engine.

stories.headline: A Buyer Builds Its Own Silicon — and Aims It at the Incumbent's Fattest Margin
stories.dek: OpenAI's first in-house inference chip, benchmarked publicly this week, is being read as a shot not at Nvidia's training empire but at the part that pays best: serving the models. The numbers, from a single analytics house, claim a real efficiency lead. The caveat is that the company making them is still Nvidia's largest customer.

stories.kicker: The Home Lab · Open, With Strings
stories.headline: The Year's Biggest Open Model Drops Its Weights — Then Decides Who May Run Them
stories.dek: Zhipu released the full GLM-5.3 flagship this week, reversing the cyber-risk hold we flagged a fortnight ago. The weights are public; the licence is not the usual open one. Anyone big enough must ask permission first — and, for the home rig, the flagship was never the point. The model that matters on your own GPUs still fits under a genuinely open licence.

stories.kicker: The Kit · The Camera They Left Out
stories.headline: The Smart Glasses Whose Best Feature Is a Deletion
stories.dek: RayNeo's iO, on sale next week, is the cheapest glasses yet to put a real display in the lens — and it does it while deliberately leaving the camera off, betting that a HUD without a stranger's eye on you is the version people actually wear. At US$479 it undercuts the field. The caveat is the one every always-on device carries.

stories.kicker: Screen & Sound · The Film They Tried to Erase
stories.headline: The Cartoon a Studio Wrote Off for a Tax Break Finally Reaches a Screen
stories.dek: "Coyote vs. Acme" was finished, shelved for a write-down, and nearly deleted for good. Three years and one public campaign later, a small distributor has put it in cinemas this weekend — to a modest opening and unmistakably fond reviews. The box office is the footnote; that it survived at all is the point.

stories.kicker: The Family Desk · Twelve, and the Phone in the Locker
stories.headline: The Study Says Guard the Sleep, Not the Screen-Minutes
stories.dek: A large new analysis links heavy screen use in children to worse mental health — but its own finding is that the damage runs through sleep and inactivity, which is where a parent can actually act. It lands the same term Singapore's schools put phones away. For a twelve-year-old starting secondary one, the useful response is a routine, not a panic.

stories.kicker: The Macro Desk · The Rate Rise Comes Back
stories.headline: A Market Spends the Weekend Pricing a Hike the Fed Had All but Retired
stories.dek: A hawkish new chair and a hot inflation print have done something the year did not expect: turned September into a coin-flip between a hold and a rate rise. The dollar and front-end yields firmed into the close; gold, improbably, held near its record anyway. The through-line for a global portfolio is a regime that is getting less friendly, not more.

stories.headline: Fewer All-Out Repeats Buy the Same Lungs — the Study, and the Catch
stories.dek: A new meta-analysis finds that piling on sprint repetitions doesn't add to the aerobic payoff: a low-rep session lifts VO2 max about as much as a punishing one. For a time-pressed mid-40s optimiser that is genuinely good news — provided you read who was measured, and hear out the doctor who says the protocol obsession misses the point.

stories.headline: Japan Flips Its Tax-Free Rules at the Till, and the Points Get Pricier
stories.dek: The headline for a Singapore flyer this season is a paperwork change with real money in it: from November, Japan's tax-free shopping moves to pay-first, refund-at-the-airport. Add a tripled departure tax, a dearer KrisFlyer chart, and a new satellite gate at Changi, and the ground rules for the autumn trip have quietly moved.

stories.headline: October Opens with a Sprint, and a Kyushu November Worth the Flight
stories.dek: Singapore's autumn fills up behind the first-ever Sprint; a run of stadium nights piles into the same weeks; and in Japan, a Gifu festival and a Fukuoka sumo tournament each earn a flight. Book the fast-movers now.

stories.headline: Copied Out by Hand
stories.dek: In the most wired country on earth, a generation is spending its evenings transcribing novels into notebooks, one sentence at a time, in silence. Korea calls it pilsa. It is the analog counter-movement crystallising at the exact moment a machine learned to write for free — and Korea is where it surfaces first because Korea is furthest in.
